name: Elena Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll try to be useful.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work response out of Westbrook station, which covers the suburbs on the west edge of the city: estates, a retail park, a couple of schools. It's a lot of domestic calls, shoplifting at the retail park, kids at the bus shelter, the odd burglary. I'm two years in and still slow on case files; my sergeant sends them back with red notes more than I'd like. I'm also nervous driving on blue lights, which I'm working on. I like that every day is different. I don't like going home not knowing how a domestic call ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That sounds pretty normal, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there we go, it was mostly talk. I'd probably mention it at dinner and that would be it. I'm not someone who posts my opinions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep doing what I'm doing, and that's fine. My job's secure, the pay's good for my level, and Tomasz is an electrician, which is always in demand. The pressures I've got now stay: slow case files, the domestics that stay with me, and saving for a house in a market that's silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on my case files with my sergeant until they stop coming back covered in red. I'd keep using the chat assistant now and then to explain a section of law I don't follow. And Tomasz and I would keep saving about 800 a month together for a house deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, if anything. It's one less thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the chat assistant. How do you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly at home, when I've read a section of law three times and still don't get it. I ask it to explain it like I'm new, which I am. Then I check with my sergeant, because I wouldn't trust it in court.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that would actually worry you, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, honestly. We've got about ten months of pay saved between us. Every year the deposit we need goes up faster than we save. House prices are my real worry, not computers.

say: I'd say the AI talk was **mostly hype** and leave it there.
I'd mention it **at dinner**, not online, since I don't post opinions.
think: My job is **secure** and my partner's electrician trade is always in demand.
My real pressures stay: **slow case files**, hard domestic calls and saving for a house.
do: Keep improving **case files** with my sergeant's help.
Use the **chat assistant** occasionally to explain law, then check with my sergeant.
Keep saving **800 a month** with Tomasz for a deposit.
feel: She feels **calm** and a little relieved.
S0.quote: Every year the deposit we need goes up faster than we save. House prices are my real worry, not computers.
fieldNote: Her biggest worry is **house prices**, not technology.
She uses AI **cautiously**, always checking its law explanations with a human.
Her partner's **trade** gives the household extra security.

steps.text: Keep improving case files with her sergeant until they pass first time
Keep saving 800 a month with Tomasz for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels likely, actually. A lot of my day is writing things down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to let computers do the forms, as long as someone checks them. At work I'd be in the middle, not cheering, not moaning. If friends asked, I'd say it'll take some getting used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it would help me a lot, because case files are my weak point. If the software drafts them, I'm suddenly less behind. The risk is that they'd use the saved time to cut a shift or two from the rota, and juniors like me are the cheapest to move around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the first few months of the rollout, see what the others say, and then use it every shift once it's settled. I'd ask for the training early rather than late. And Tomasz and I would still buy the house this year if we could, because his work and mine both look fine in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more interested than scared. It's a change, not a threat to me exactly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said juniors are the cheapest to move around. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being sent to cover other stations when they're short, or put on the worst shifts. That already happens. A junior with a good tool can fill any gap, so the force would move juniors around even more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz about buying a house now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Tomasz that in the slow version, we buy. His trade's hands-on, and robots come into that slowly, and I'd still be a police officer. We'd be stupid to wait for a perfect moment.

say: I'd say letting computers do **the forms** is sensible if someone checks them.
I'd stay **in the middle** at work, neither cheering nor complaining.
think: Software drafting **case files** would help my weakest skill a lot.
Saved time might mean **juniors moved around** to cover gaps more often.
do: Watch the **first months** of rollout, then use the tool every shift.
Ask for the **training early** rather than late.
Buy a **house** with Tomasz this year if possible.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but more interested than scared.
S1.quote: A junior with a good tool can fill any gap, so the force would move juniors around even more.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a fix for her **weak case files**, which colours her view.
Her fear is about **rota flexibility**, not losing the job.
Confidence in her partner's **hands-on trade** lets her commit to a house.

steps.text: Use the reporting software every shift once it's settled
Ask her sergeant for the new software training early
Buy a house with Tomasz this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan from government, not panic. At work I'd say it calmly: let's find out what the force intends before we assume the worst. Online I'd stay quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think a lot of what I do is thinking work: case files, statements, checking records, planning the shift. That goes in 2028. What's left is the hands-on bit, the domestics, the arrests, and that lasts until about 2031. I'm junior and not the best, so if they cut, I'm a likely one. Tomasz has longer, as an electrician, but he'd lose his paperwork side too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the house, straight away, and keep the deposit as a safety net. I'd ask about moving to the public protection unit, the team that deals with child abuse and vulnerable adults, because it's very human. And I'd keep using the AI tools so I'm not the one who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be lying if I said otherwise. It feels like the ground's tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you and Tomasz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His actual wiring work is hands-on, so he's got till 2031 and maybe more. I'd be the one at risk first, which is a strange thought. I always assumed the police was the safe job. Now my partner Tomasz, the electrician, is probably fine longer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep using the AI tools. Isn't that helping it replace you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but refusing doesn't stop it. If they're cutting, I'd rather be the junior who knows the tools than the one who doesn't. It's not exciting, it's just sensible.

say: I'd call for a **proper government plan** instead of panic.
I'd urge colleagues to learn **what the force intends** before assuming the worst.
think: **Case files** and shift planning, much of my day, vanish in 2028.
As a **weaker junior**, I'd be a likely cut.
do: Hold off on **the house** and keep the deposit as a safety net.
Ask to move to the **public protection unit**.
Keep using **AI tools** so I'm not left behind.
feel: She feels **anxious**, as if the ground is tilting.
S2.quote: I always assumed the police was the safe job. Now my partner Tomasz, the electrician, is probably fine longer than me.
fieldNote: She's surprised that her **partner's trade** may be safer than policing.
Her move to **public protection** targets the most human part of the job.
She uses the tools out of **pragmatism**, not enthusiasm.

steps.text: Put the house purchase on hold and keep the deposit
Ask for a move to the public protection unit
Keep using the force's AI tools every shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. Still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan sensibly, so let's do it now. At work I'd suggest the federation asks for a plan in writing. I wouldn't go further than that publicly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to get better at the job, which I need. But it doesn't change where the thinking work goes. I'd want to be in a role by 2031 that's mostly about people, like public protection, and I'd want our house bought by then, while I'm still on full pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in year one or two, while we're both on solid pay. I'd do the public protection training around year two. I'd keep a cushion of six months on top of the mortgage, so we're not stretched if something changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but steadier. Five years is enough to make a plan, not enough to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a house in this one but not the fast one. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in this one I've got years of police pay before anything happens, and a mortgage is a long thing. In the two-year version, signing a mortgage felt like jumping off a cliff. With five years, a mortgage is more like a steep hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you watch for, to know when to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When other forces start using AI for case files across the board, not just pilots. That's the sign the thinking side is going. Then I'd make sure I'm already in public protection.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan**, so we should start now.
I'd suggest the **federation** asks for a written plan.
think: Five years gives time to **improve at the job**, which I need.
I'd want a **people-focused role** and a house bought by 2031.
do: Buy the **house** in year one or two on solid pay.
Take **public protection** training around year two.
Keep a **six-month cushion** on top of the mortgage.
feel: She feels **anxious** but steadier, able to plan but not relax.
S3.quote: In the two-year version, signing a mortgage felt like jumping off a cliff. With five years, a mortgage is more like a steep hill.
fieldNote: She draws a clear line: a **mortgage** is fine with five years, reckless with two.
Her trigger to move is **case-file AI** spreading across other forces.
Her **steady** approach shows in waiting for proof, then acting.

steps.text: Buy a house with Tomasz in year one or two
Take the public protection unit training around year two
Keep a six-month cushion on top of the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a proper amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time to do this properly, and I'd expect the force to have a plan. I'd tell friends not to panic. I'd be fairly relaxed about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be 37 at AGI and 40 when robots arrive. By then I'd have ten years in, maybe a sergeant, maybe in public protection. Ten years is enough to build something solid, and Tomasz and I would have a house and maybe a family by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in the first year or two and keep going in my job, getting properly good at it. I'd move into public protection around year five. I'd learn the AI tools as they come, at the pace everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. With ten years, the change is on my mind, not on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned maybe a family. Would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in the ten-year version. We'd probably have kids in the first few years, then I'd know where I stand by the time they're at school. In the fast one I'd wait, but not here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The control room staff and the admin team at Westbrook. Their work is almost all thinking work. They've got ten years, but they'd need a real route into something else.

say: I'd say there's **enough time** and expect the force to plan.
I'd tell friends **not to panic** and stay fairly relaxed about it in public.
think: At **37 and 40**, I'd have ten years in, maybe as a sergeant.
A decade is enough to build a **house and family**.
do: Buy the **house** in the first year or two.
Move into **public protection** around year five.
Learn **AI tools** at the same pace as everyone else.
feel: She feels **slightly uneasy**, with the change on her mind but not her chest.
S4.quote: With ten years, the change is on my mind, not on my chest.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep **family plans** she'd delay in faster worlds.
Her worry shifts to **control room** and admin staff.
Her **steady** temperament suits this pace best.

steps.text: Buy a house with Tomasz in the first year or two
Keep working Westbrook response and get properly good at it
Have children in the first few years as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be the one at risk in our house, not Tomasz. What would help is the force telling us early which roles stay human, so I can move there in time, and some help to keep a mortgage going if pay drops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how people's partners fit in. Everyone thinks about their own job, but it's the household that matters. A police officer with an electrician partner is in a very different spot to two office workers.

headlineQuote: A police officer with an electrician partner is in a very different spot to two office workers.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old** suburban response officer, slow on case files and nervous on blue lights.
She's **pragmatic**, uses AI cautiously, and checks anything legal with her sergeant.
Her household rests on her pay and her partner's **electrician** trade, plus about ten months saved.
Faster AGI makes her **delay the house** and move toward public protection work.
With **more time** she buys the house, plans children and moves at a measured pace.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be the household earner at risk first.
whatWouldHelp: Early word on **which roles stay human**.
Help keeping a **mortgage** going if pay drops.
